title: A clear opening
hook: We have given you a clear victory, an opening, after Hudaybiyyah (48:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tadabbur, following a verse past its last word, and your line was unlock the heart. What did you read slowly? Day five hundred eighty.

The biographies place it in the sixth year after the move to Medina. About fourteen hundred Muslims, by the reports, set out from Medina toward Mecca, dressed as pilgrims, with animals for sacrifice and no intention of fighting. They want to perform the lesser pilgrimage, the 'umrah. They get as far as a place called Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred land, and the Quraysh block the road. What follows is a treaty that, to many of the Muslims there, felt like losing. And on the way home, a surah arrives calling it a victory.

Look at the terms, as the hadith and biographies report them. The Muslims would turn back this year and come next year instead. A truce of ten years. Anyone who came from Mecca to the Muslims without permission would be sent back; anyone who went the other way would not. Even the writing of the treaty stung: the Meccan envoy refused the words Messenger of God, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ agreed to sign as Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah. 'Umar, by his own later account in Sahih al-Bukhari, went to the Prophet and asked: are we not in the right? Why accept this? Then, on the road back to Medina, Surah Al-Fath was revealed. Pickthall translates its first verse: "Lo! We have given thee (O Muhammad) a signal victory." The Arabic word is fath, and its first meaning is opening, like a door. Fath mubin: a clear opening. Bukhari records that the Prophet said a surah had come to him that night dearer to him than everything the sun rises upon. How could a treaty like that be an opening? The truce meant people could travel, trade and talk freely. Ibn Ishaq passes on the view of al-Zuhri, an early historian, that more people entered Islam in the two years after the truce than in all the years before it. The biographies tell how the following year the pilgrimage happened, peacefully, and how within two years Mecca itself opened, almost without a fight. The companions who'd felt defeated came to see Hudaybiyyah as the hinge. The surah didn't change the treaty's terms. It changed what they were looking at: not the door that closed, but the one that was opening.
screen: `TERMS THAT STUNG.` · `'UMAR: WHY ACCEPT THIS?` · `FATH: AN OPENING, LIKE A DOOR.` · `THE TRUCE BECAME THE HINGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: look for the opening in a closure. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a door that closed on you: a job you didn't get, a plan that fell through, a no you're still sore about. Don't rush to make it good. Just hold it. Then ask, gently: did anything become possible because of it? A road, a person, a quiet? If nothing yet, that's honest too. If you pray, you can ask to see the opening. The bell holds the time.
A clear opening. Fath mubin: the name 48:1 gives the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, a closing that turned out to be a door. Today's word.
Your line: an opening. Today, when something doesn't go your way, before you react, say one word to yourself: opening. Then look around once. Day five hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Hudaybiyyah as a lesson in patience and trust, and many recite Surah Al-Fath when hoping for a way through a hard situation.

fork.setup: you are at Hudaybiyyah. the terms send you home without the pilgrimage. what does the surah revealed on the way back call it?
fork.reveal: 48:1 calls it fath mubin. the truce opened the roads, and Mecca opened within two years.

original.note: Arabic: a clear opening, a manifest victory (48:1).

trapdoor: what you thought: victory means winning a battle.
what it means: an opening, here a treaty that looked like a loss and became the turning point.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari records 'Umar's objection and the Prophet calling this surah dearer than all the sun rises on.
